cards.statement: A TCP server distinguishes clients sharing an IP address using their source ports.
cards.explanation: TCP identifies connections by both endpoints' addresses and ports.

source.title: Improving TCP's Robustness to Blind In-Window Attacks

cards.statement: A TCP server's SYN-ACK acknowledges its own SYN during the handshake.
cards.explanation: The TCP server's SYN-ACK acknowledges the client's SYN.
cards.misconception: SYN-ACK acknowledges the sender's own SYN.

source.title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

cards.statement: A TCP sender counts its SYN as one sequence position even with an empty payload.
cards.explanation: Sequencing the TCP SYN makes retransmission and duplicate detection work during setup.

source.title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

cards.statement: TCP should derive initial sequence numbers from a clock plus a keyed function.
cards.explanation: Keyed generation makes TCP initial sequence numbers harder to predict.

source.title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

cards.statement: A TCP endpoint advertises its maximum outgoing TCP payload in the MSS option.
cards.explanation: A TCP endpoint advertises its maximum receivable payload in MSS.
cards.misconception: An advertised MSS describes the sender's transmit capacity.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

cards.statement: A TCP endpoint in CLOSE-WAIT awaits its local application's request to close the connection.
cards.explanation: CLOSE-WAIT follows the peer's FIN; TCP awaits the local application's close request.

source.title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

cards.statement: After a TCP peer sends FIN, the other peer can still send data on that connection.
cards.explanation: TCP closes its sending directions independently, so one direction can remain open.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

cards.statement: A TCP endpoint sends RST as the final confirmation of an orderly FIN exchange.
cards.explanation: A TCP RST aborts a connection, abandoning queued data rather than completing an orderly close.
cards.misconception: RST confirms a graceful FIN exchange.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

cards.statement: A TCP peer in SYN-SENT may reject a valid peer SYN because both peers initiate the connection.
cards.explanation: TCP supports simultaneous open, letting two active peers complete connection establishment.
cards.misconception: Crossed SYNs force an active open to fail.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

cards.statement: In a sequential TCP close, the peer that receives the first FIN takes the TIME-WAIT role.
cards.explanation: For an orderly TCP close, the first FIN sender takes TIME-WAIT as the active closer.
cards.misconception: The passive closer retains TIME-WAIT.

source.title: TIME-WAIT Assassination Hazards in TCP

cards.statement: TCP must set its TIME-WAIT timer to twice the Maximum Segment Lifetime.
cards.explanation: TCP's TIME-WAIT lets delayed segments expire and retains state to acknowledge a retransmitted FIN after a lost final ACK.

source.title: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

cards.statement: A TCP implementation enables keep-alive probes by default for an idle connection.
cards.explanation: TCP keep-alives are optional; implementations that include them start with probing disabled.
cards.misconception: Keep-alive probing starts enabled.

source.title: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

cards.statement: A TCP receiver preserves the boundaries between separate writes made by the sending application.
cards.explanation: TCP transports bytes; receiving applications supply their own message framing.
cards.misconception: TCP preserves application write boundaries.

source.title: RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

cards.statement: A TCP sender advances data sequence numbers by payload bytes rather than by segment count.
cards.explanation: Sequence positions track bytes across segmentation and retransmission.

source.title: RFC 7323: TCP Extensions for High Performance

cards.statement: A TCP receiver can advance its cumulative ACK past a missing byte when later data arrives.
cards.explanation: A cumulative ACK covers the uninterrupted received prefix; its number identifies the next expected byte.
cards.misconception: A cumulative ACK covers data beyond gaps.

source.title: RFC 2018: TCP Selective Acknowledgment Options

cards.statement: A TCP receiver can use SACK to report received byte ranges separated by gaps in the data.
cards.explanation: SACK blocks describe received ranges, helping the sender avoid resending data that arrived.

source.title: RFC 2018: TCP Selective Acknowledgment Options

cards.statement: A TCP sender replaces its smoothed round-trip estimate with the latest measured round-trip time.
cards.explanation: TCP blends new RTT samples with its existing estimate and includes variation when calculating its retransmission timeout.
cards.misconception: The latest RTT measurement replaces the running estimate.

source.title: RFC 6298: Computing TCP's Retransmission Timer

cards.statement: TCP classic fast retransmit resends a suspected missing segment after three consecutive duplicate ACKs.
cards.explanation: The duplicate ACK pattern triggers retransmission before the retransmission timer expires.

source.title: RFC 5681: TCP Congestion Control

cards.statement: A TCP receiver advertises its receive window to report the network path's capacity for more data.
cards.explanation: The receive window limits outstanding data according to what the receiving endpoint is prepared to accept.
cards.misconception: The receive window describes available network capacity.

source.title: RFC 5681: TCP Congestion Control

cards.statement: A TCP receiver can use Window Scale to advertise larger receive windows than its base header field represents.
cards.explanation: The negotiated scale factor expands the receive-window value carried in subsequent TCP headers.

source.title: RFC 7323: TCP Extensions for High Performance

cards.statement: A TCP sender uses the larger of its congestion and receive windows to limit outstanding data.
cards.explanation: The smaller of cwnd and rwnd governs outstanding data, respecting both limits together.
cards.misconception: The larger window determines the sending limit.

source.title: RFC 5681: TCP Congestion Control

cards.statement: A TCP sender uses slow start while its congestion window is below the slow start threshold.
cards.explanation: The threshold determines when the sender changes to congestion avoidance as its window grows.

source.title: RFC 5681: TCP Congestion Control

cards.statement: A TCP implementation must let an application disable the Nagle algorithm on an individual connection.
cards.explanation: Nagle coalesces small sends; applications have a connection-specific switch for that behavior.

source.title: RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers

cards.statement: A TCP receiver can deliver later bytes to the application while an earlier byte remains missing.
cards.explanation: TCP delays later application data until the gap is filled, preserving delivery order.
cards.misconception: TCP delivers application data beyond gaps.

source.title: RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)

cards.statement: A DNS client treats www.example.net. as a name relative to its configured search domain.
cards.explanation: The trailing dot represents the root label, so www.example.net. is an absolute name rather than a name to extend with a local suffix.
cards.misconception: A trailing dot leaves a DNS name relative to a search domain.

source.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities

cards.statement: A DNS server matches the ASCII names API.example.net and api.example.net as the same domain name.
cards.explanation: DNS comparison treats ASCII uppercase and lowercase letters as equivalent, even when a server preserves their original appearance.

source.title: RFC 4343: Domain Name System (DNS) Case Insensitivity Clarification

cards.statement: A DNS resolver treats a delegated child's ordinary data as part of the parent zone's authority.
cards.explanation: A delegation separates a child's authoritative data from the parent zone. The child zone's authoritative servers supply its ordinary records.
cards.misconception: A parent zone remains authoritative for a child's ordinary data after delegation.

source.title: RFC 1034: Domain Names - Concepts and Facilities

cards.statement: A DNS stub resolver hands a lookup to a recursive resolver to obtain the final answer.
cards.explanation: A stub resolver depends on a recursive resolver to perform the resolution work it lacks the capability to complete itself.

source.title: RFC 9499: DNS Terminology

cards.statement: In iterative DNS resolution, a resolver follows a referral by querying the server it points toward.
cards.explanation: A referral directs the resolver toward another server. The resolver pursues the lookup there instead of having the referring server finish it.

source.title: RFC 9499: DNS Terminology

cards.statement: IANA describes the DNS root service as named authorities running across hundreds of servers.
cards.explanation: The root service spreads its named authorities over many server instances, rather than one machine per authority.
cards.volatilityNote: The number and distribution of deployed root-server instances can change.

source.title: IANA: Root Servers

cards.statement: A DNS resolver applies one response-wide TTL when caching records from the same reply.
cards.explanation: DNS gives resource records their own TTLs, so records from one response can have different cache lifetimes.
cards.misconception: A DNS response has a single cache lifetime shared by its records.

source.title: RFC 1035: Domain Names - Implementation and Specification

cards.statement: A DNS resolver can cache a record received with TTL zero for later lookups by default.
cards.explanation: TTL zero confines a DNS record's use to the current transaction; the resolver should not cache it for later lookups.
cards.misconception: A record received with TTL zero remains reusable across transactions.

source.title: RFC 8767: Serving Stale Data to Improve DNS Resiliency

cards.statement: A DNS resolver uses the SOA MINIMUM field alone to set a negative answer's cache lifetime.
cards.explanation: For NXDOMAIN and NODATA, the negative-cache TTL is the smaller of SOA MINIMUM and the SOA record's TTL.
cards.misconception: SOA MINIMUM alone determines the negative-cache lifetime.

source.title: RFC 2308: Negative Caching of DNS Queries (DNS NCACHE)

cards.statement: A DNS resolver can serve expired cached records when it fails to refresh them from authoritative servers.
cards.explanation: Serve-stale permits a resolver to use expired data during a refresh failure, preserving answers through temporary authoritative-server outages.

source.title: RFC 8767: Serving Stale Data to Improve DNS Resiliency

cards.statement: A general-purpose DNS implementation must support TCP for queries as well as UDP.
cards.explanation: TCP support forms part of general-purpose DNS service, including ordinary queries; it is more than a transport for zone transfers.

source.title: RFC 7766: DNS Transport over TCP - Implementation Requirements

cards.statement: A DNS requester uses EDNS(0) to advertise how large a DNS response its TCP connection accepts.
cards.explanation: EDNS(0) advertises the requester's capacity for larger UDP responses, allowing them to remain on UDP instead of requiring a TCP retry.
cards.misconception: EDNS(0) advertises a TCP response-size limit.

source.title: RFC 6891: Extension Mechanisms for DNS (EDNS(0))

cards.statement: A DNS server groups A and AAAA records with the same owner name into one RRset.
cards.explanation: A DNS RRset groups records with the same owner, class and type; A and AAAA belong to separate sets.
cards.misconception: Matching owner names merge different record types.

source.title: Clarifications to the DNS Specification

cards.statement: A resolver reads an IPv4 address from the RDATA of an AAAA record.
cards.explanation: An AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address for its owner name.
cards.misconception: AAAA supplies IPv4 address data.

source.title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6

cards.statement: A zone administrator places a CNAME at the zone apex alongside its SOA and NS records.
cards.explanation: A zone apex holds SOA and NS records, which conflict with CNAME coexistence rules; DNSSEC records are the exception.
cards.misconception: A zone apex accepts CNAME alongside its required records.

source.title: Clarifications to the DNS Specification

cards.statement: A mail sender prefers a lower MX preference value when choosing among a domain's mail exchangers.
cards.explanation: MX preference ranks mail exchangers in ascending order, so smaller values get tried first.

source.title: Domain Names - Implementation and Specification

cards.statement: A domain administrator points an MX target directly at a CNAME so mail senders follow the alias.
cards.explanation: An ordinary MX target names a host with address records; the target must not be an alias.
cards.misconception: Mail exchanger targets can be CNAME aliases.

source.title: Clarifications to the DNS Specification

cards.statement: A mail sender stops delivery attempts to a domain that publishes a Null MX.
cards.explanation: Null MX declares that a domain accepts no mail, so senders avoid retries and fallback delivery.

source.title: A 'Null MX' No Service Resource Record for Domains That Accept No Mail

cards.statement: A DNS primary uses the SOA serial to identify the version of its zone data.
cards.explanation: The serial marks a zone's data version and changes when that version changes.

source.title: Domain Names - Implementation and Specification

cards.statement: A domain administrator publishes an SPF policy as a TXT record at the domain name.
cards.explanation: SPF puts a sender-authorization policy in TXT data for the domain being evaluated.

source.title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) for Authorizing Use of Domains in Email, Version 1

cards.statement: An IPv6 reverse-DNS lookup searches for PTR records beneath in-addr.arpa.
cards.explanation: PTR lookups for IPv6 addresses use the ip6.arpa reverse tree.
cards.misconception: IPv6 reverse lookups share IPv4's reverse tree.

source.title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6

cards.statement: An SRV-aware client learns the destination port from the service's SRV record.
cards.explanation: SRV data includes the service's port as well as its target host, so clients can use the advertised port.

source.title: A DNS RR for specifying the location of services (DNS SRV)

cards.statement: A service administrator uses SVCB AliasMode for aliasing at a zone apex.
cards.explanation: SVCB AliasMode provides apex-compatible aliasing for protocols that use SVCB; it does not redirect arbitrary protocols.

source.title: Service Binding and Parameter Specification via the DNS (SVCB and HTTPS Resource Records)

cards.statement: An authoritative DNS server guarantees a complete record listing in its response to an ANY query.
cards.explanation: An authoritative server may answer ANY with a small subset or synthesized response; ANY does not promise an exhaustive record listing.
cards.misconception: An ANY response guarantees an exhaustive record list.

source.title: Providing Minimal-Sized Responses to DNS Queries That Have QTYPE=ANY
